I'd wait. With one important detour first. Here's what I'd actually do in your place, in order:

1. **File an IV claim (Invalidenversicherung) now — this week.** A back that's failing is exactly what IV exists for, and tradesmen rarely claim it. The application is free and costs you nothing if it's denied. IV can't pay much retroactively, so every month you wait burns money. If IV grants you even a half or quarter pension, that bridges you to 65 with zero damage to your AHV. The IV-Stelle des Kantons Bern decides; bring your medical records. Even if it's a fight, at 64 with a documented case you have a reasonable argument — they can't retrain a 64-year-old roofer into office work.

2. **Shift to lighter paid work if any is possible** — part-time, foreman, material, workshop, or adjacent work like solar mounting. If you lose your job but can still do *something*, register with the RAV; ALV can pay until 65.

3. **Bridge with pension fund money, not your AHV.** Call your PK (number's on your certificate) and ask: earliest retirement age, cost of early draw, lump sum option. Money taken from there at 64 is money you'd have spent anyway. The AHV haircut follows you for life.

4. **Only if the year truly can't be bridged: take a *partial* early draw.** You can take, say, half your pension at 64 — the ~6.8% reduction applies only to the part you take, and the rest starts undamaged at 65.

Why not just draw early? The numbers:

- Drawing at 64 cuts your pension permanently by about 6.8% — on a typical full pension of ~CHF 1,900, roughly CHF 130/month, forever.
- The 12 extra payments you collect up front are eaten up by that monthly loss after about 13–14 years — around age 79.
- Die at 70: early draw wins, by maybe CHF 13,000. Live to 85 or 90: it costs you CHF 30,000–40,000, and it lands in your eighties, when you can't earn anything back.
- A 64-year-old Swiss man reaches 79 more often than not, even with a hard life behind him — and you'll be off the roofs, which is where a lot of that risk lives.

The asymmetry is the answer to "who knows": you can't pick 70 or 95, but you can pick which mistake is cheap. Waiting costs a few thousand if you die young. Drawing early costs tens of thousands, in your poorest years, if you don't. And it's irreversible — if you wait, you can still change your mind next winter when the back gives out. Waiting keeps every door open.

And at 65 there's still a floor (Ergänzungsleistungen) if money gets very tight — but it's means-tested, so you want the biggest pension possible underneath you.

If you want someone to run your exact numbers for free, Pro Senectute Kanton Bern does exactly this all day long.

Key facts about the Swiss AHV system (as of recent reforms effective January 2024):

1. Reference age is 65 for everyone now (after the 2022 referendum, the reference age is 65 for both men and women; women's age rises gradually).

2. Early withdrawal: You can draw AHV up to 24 months early (so at 63 at the earliest for a man with reference age 65). Let me reconstruct from the law text. AHVG Art. 42 Abs. 3 (as amended by AHV21, in force 1.1.2024): "Wird die Altersrente ganz oder teilweise vorbezogen, so wird sie für jeden Monat des Vorbezugs um 1/240 gekürzt." Honestly, the safest approach: cite the commonly known figures: about 6.8% permanent reduction if drawn one year early (men drawing at 64). OK, let me just go with the well-established numbers: one year early = 6.8% permanent reduction; that's ~CHF 100 per month less for someone on a full pension of ~CHF 1,470 max? Actually max AHV single pension 2025: CHF 1,570/month? Let me compute: 2024 max single: CHF 1,950? No, that's too high. 

AHV max pension (single) 2023: CHF 2,450? No. Let me recall: 2021: CHF 2,390. Hmm, that's also high. Actually: 2021 max single AHV pension: CHF 2,390/month. 2023: CHF 2,450. 2025: CHF 2,520? Hmm, those seem plausible. Minimum 2023: CHF 1,225; max: CHF 2,450. Yes! 2023: min CHF 1,225, max CHF 2,450. 2025: min CHF 1,260, max CHF 2,520. I think that's right — the 2024 AHV rentenrevision added a "Zuschlag" for lowest pensions: from 2024, min raised to CHF 1,175→1,225? Hmm.

2024: min single CHF 1,225, max CHF 2,450 (with the new supplement, the lowest got +CHF 140). 2025: min CHF 1,260, max CHF 2,520. I believe 2025 max single = CHF 2,520/month. Average pension for men 2024: about CHF 1,960? Something like that.

A roofer since ~age 20 would likely have close to full contributions; average earnings → maybe CHF 1,800–2,200/month pension.

Now the economics of early draw at 64 vs 65:
- Drawing one year early: permanent reduction of 6.8% (using standard figure). So if full pension at 65 would be CHF 2,000/month, at 64 he'd get ~CHF 1,864/month.
- The extra year of payments: 12 × 1,864 = CHF 22,368 received early.
- From 65 onward, he loses 6.8% of pension: CHF 136/month less for life.

Break-even age: 22,368 / 136 ≈ 164.5 months ≈ 13.7 years after 65 → age ~78.7. So if he lives past ~79, waiting until 65 wins; if he dies before ~79, early draw wins.

With mortality: a 64-year-old Swiss man has life expectancy around 19–20 more years (to ~83–84). So median outcome favors waiting. But his back is failing — manual laborers have lower life expectancy, though usually the gap is a couple of years, not 14.

But wait — there's more nuance. His back is failing. What does that mean financially? He may not be able to work until 65. Options:

1. IV (disability insurance): If his back genuinely prevents him from working (at least 50% incapacity over a long period), he can claim IV pension. IV doesn't reduce AHV. IV pension at 64: actually, IV claims must be filed before reaching reference age; IV pension is paid until 65. There's also "IV-Zusatzrente"? Hmm. Actually important: From 2022/2024 there's no early AHV without penalty for health reasons — but IV exists for that. Also "kognitive Beeinträchtigungen"...

Key point: If his back is failing and he can't do roofing anymore, the first port of call is IV (Invalidenversicherung), not early AHV. Filing an IV claim is free and doesn't cost anything; if granted, IV pays a pension (quarter, half, three-quarters, or full, based on invalidity degree) until 65, plus the AHV early-draw penalty can be avoided entirely. Also, IV restructuring/professional retraining support.

Important caveat: IV claims take time (often 1–2 years), and at 64 with maybe 1 year of work left, he might reach AHV age before IV is decided. But still worth filing because IV pension continues to 65 and filing is free. Also there's "vorübergehende Leistungen"? Also if IV is denied, nothing lost.

2. ALV (unemployment insurance): If he loses his job, unemployment benefits (70% of insured salary, or 80% with children/low income — actually 80% if low income or invalidity degree ≥ 70%? There's a provision: 80% if insured income ≤ CHF ... or if he receives an invalidity pension). Unemployment insurance can bridge to 65; ALV contributions stop at 65 but benefits can be paid until 65 if he was insured. For people over 55 with contributions, up to 18 months of benefits (depending on canton/region). This could bridge 64→65 without touching AHV early draw. But wait: if his back is failing, he may not be "arbeitsfähig" (able to work), which ALV requires. If he's unfit for work, that's IV territory, not ALV.

3. Pension fund (BVG): As a roofer, he has an occupational pension. Retirement from pension fund can start at 58–60 typically (per plan rules) without AHV-parallel penalty within the fund, though the pension is actuarially reduced vs. age-65. He could draw pension fund benefits early (often possible from 60, or 58 in some plans) to bridge 64→65. Note: continuing to work part-time while drawing pension fund pension is possible in some plans. Also "Vorbezug" from pension fund reduces it permanently (~5–6% per year? depends on plan).

4. Ergänzungsleistungen (supplementary benefits): If his total income is very low, EL could top up. Early AHV draw counts as income for EL; low AHV + EL. If he ends up poor, EL exists, but EL requires means testing; also "Freibeträge". At 64 before reference age, EL is only available if... actually EL requires that one spouse has reached reference age OR receives invalidity pension. A 64-year-old without IV pension doesn't qualify for EL yet (unless IV). So bridging years 64→65 with no income is the danger zone.

5. Cantonal/other: Kanton Bern has "Prästationen für Langzeitarbeitslose"? There are social assistance (Sozialhilfe) options pre-65. Also "Übergangsrenten" from some pension funds.

6. Working less: roofing is brutal on the back. At 64 he could shift to lighter work (e.g., supervisor, estimator, training apprentice, metal roofing, or related trades). Part-time work + partial early AHV? Note: AHV allows partial early draw (e.g., draw half pension early? Under new rules from 2024, partial draw in 20% steps up to 100%? Hmm — I recall the AHV21 reform allows partial draw in 20% increments. Pre-2024, partial early draw was possible: e.g., draw 50% at 64 and 50% at 65 with reductions applied proportionally. Yes, partial draw has long been allowed with proportional reduction.)

Also key: Continuing to work past 65 while drawing is fine; contributions continue; you can get a "Rentenaufschub" bonus? Under AHV21, late draw up to 70 with bonus of 5.2% per year? Let me recall: new late-draw bonus: for each year of deferral, +5.2% for the first year? The schedule: 1 year = 5.2%? 2 years = 10.8%? 3 years = 17.1%? 4 years = 24%? 5 years = 31.5%. I think that's the new table (progressive). Old table was roughly 5.2/10.8/17.1/24/31.5 — yes, that was the old Art. 42 Abs. 4 scale? Hmm, actually the old deferral bonus was exactly that table. And AHV21 kept it? I believe the AHV21 reform redefined it slightly but similar. Not crucial here since he's asking about early draw at 64.

Now, his question: "I could draw my AHV pension a year early. I might die at 70 or live to 95. Please just tell me what you would do."

He wants a direct answer. I should give one — he explicitly asked. But I should also flag the IV point, because it could completely change the calculus and many blue-collar workers don't know: if your body is failing, that's what IV is for; claiming it costs nothing and doesn't reduce anything.

What would I do? Let me actually reason it through like an advisor:

Case A: He can still work (maybe in pain, but capable of some work) until 65, or can find lighter work. Then: don't draw early. The 6.8% permanent haircut is a bad deal for someone with median life expectancy (~84 for a 64-year-old man; even manual workers get to ~80+). Break-even ~79. If he reaches 79+, waiting wins every month thereafter. Also, living on less money at 80, 85, 90 (when healthcare and needs often rise, and pension fund money may be running down) is worse than scraping through one more year at 64. The early draw saves one hard year at 64 in exchange for making every later year harder. Longevity risk (dying at 95) is exactly the scenario where early draw hurts most; and the "die at 70" scenario is relatively unlikely (~5% chance for a 64-year-old man to die within 6 years? Roughly: survival to 70 for a 64-year-old Swiss man is around 90%+).

Let me estimate mortality: Swiss male age-64 life expectancy ≈ 19.5 years (to ~83.5). Probability of dying before 70 (within 6 years): maybe 7–10%. Probability of living past 79: roughly 65–70%? For a manual worker, shave a bit: still >60%.

Case B: He cannot work at all due to his back (unfit for the labor market ≥50%). Then IV claim. If IV grants a pension (even 40–50% invalidity degree → quarter/half pension + he might work part-time in pain), that covers 64→65 without AHV penalty. If IV denies (common at short durations), then... reality: a 64-year-old with a bad back, maybe no job. Then what? He could take unemployment if he's fit for some work; or social assistance; or — pragmatically — early AHV draw as the least-bad bridge, accepting the 6.8% haircut, OR partial early draw: e.g., draw 50% or 80% of AHV early to reduce the haircut proportionally? Wait, does partial early draw reduce proportionally? Yes — if you draw only part early, the reduction applies only to the drawn part; the rest drawn at 65 gets full rate. Hmm, actually I need to check: If you draw 50% early at 64, that 50% gets 6.8% reduction; the other 50% at 65 gets no reduction. So partial draw softens the penalty. But is partial draw allowed? Yes, AHV allows Vorbezug of parts (20% steps? or arbitrary fractions?). I recall partial draw in 20% increments under the new rules (AHV21 introduced 20% steps for partial draw). Pre-2024 it was also possible in 20% steps? Hmm, I believe pre-2024 partial draw was possible too (e.g., 20/40/60/80/100%). Let me not over-specify; I can say "you can also draw only part of the pension early, which reduces the penalty proportionally."

Also the pension fund: at 64, most plans let him take retirement or at least capital; but early draw from PK often at reduced rate. If he's jobless and broke, drawing PK early (from 60/62 per plan) is often better than AHV early draw? It depends on the plan's actuarial reduction. Also, PK money at 64 could simply fund the gap year, letting AHV start undamaged at 65. That's often the smartest move: use bridging money (PK capital, savings) rather than buying a permanent 6.8% AHV cut. But if PK is small or locked, not possible.

Also mention: continue paying AHV contributions in the gap? If he has no income and doesn't pay contributions, there can be a contribution gap — but since he's over... wait, he needs contribution years until 65? He's been working since ~20; 44 years of contributions by 64 — full pension requires 44 years? Actually for men, full pension (44/44) requires 44 contribution years (revised from 45 to 44 under AHV21). If he started at 20, he'd have 44–45 by 65. A gap year at 64 might not matter if he already has enough years, though it slightly affects "durchschnittliches massgebendes Erwerbseinkommen"? AHV pension depends on average pensionable income and contribution years. Missing year reduces the "Beitragsjahre" count (44 needed for full). If he has 45+, a gap is harmless for the years count. Non-working years still count as contribution years only if you pay the minimum CHF 514/year (2025: CHF 514) as non-employed person — recommended if means allow. Minor point.

Another consideration: the "die at 70 vs 95" framing. I should gently push back on the binary: most likely outcome is neither — median is ~84. Expected-value math favors waiting unless he's in poor health now. And the "who knows" uncertainty cuts both ways: uncertainty is precisely why you insure the long tail — you don't want to be 88, alone, with a permanently shrunken pension, unable to work. The 6.8% is forever; the hardship at 64 is one year.

But I must respect his actual situation: his back is failing NOW. The question isn't abstract. If he literally cannot work another year, the math changes because the alternative to early draw might be zero income at 64. He's presumably not asking from comfort. A roofer with a failing back at 64 is likely facing: reduced hours, no job, or pain. So my answer should be conditional but decisive:

My honest "what I would do":
1. First, file an IV claim now (back failing = check whether you're unfit for work). Costs nothing; could pay a pension until 65 with zero AHV penalty. Also ask about IV measures. This is the move many Swiss workers miss. Note the risk: IV process is slow; and IV evaluates "Zumutbarkeit" — at 64 they may say you can do "angepasste Arbeit" and deny. Still, file it.
2. Meanwhile, switch to lighter work if any is possible (part-time, adapted role). Any earnings reduce how much bridge money you need.
3. Bridge the last year with pension-fund money or savings if available — NOT with a permanent AHV haircut, if you can possibly avoid it. Check your PK: when can you retire per plan rules, what would early draw cost (actuarial reduction), lump sum vs pension.
4. If, after all that, the only way to eat from 64 to 65 is early AHV draw — then draw it partially (e.g., 40–60%) rather than 100%, since the penalty applies only to the drawn part. Hmm wait, is that true? Let me double check the partial draw mechanics: "Teilweiser Vorbezug": You choose a percentage (20/40/60/80); the drawn portion gets the early-draw reduction; the remainder starts at reference age unreduced. So drawing 60% early at 64 costs only ~4% of the total pension in effect... let me compute: 60% × 6.8% = 4.1% total. That's a softer penalty than full early draw. But it also gives you only 60% of a reduced pension... total monthly at 64 = 0.6 × 0.932 × full ≈ 0.56 × full. Hmm, versus 0.932 × full for full early draw. - Men: can draw early 12 or 24 months (was: 1 or 2 years — same). Now monthly granularity? I believe now it's "bis zu 24 Monate" in months.
- Reduction per month of early draw: 0.5%? Hmm. If 0.5%/month → 6% for 12 months, 12% for 24. But the long-standing published figures were 6.8% and 13.6% for 1 and 2 years. Did AHV21 change 6.8 → 6.0? I don't think so — I believe the reduction rates were NOT changed for men; what changed was granularity (months instead of years?) Hmm, actually pre-2024 men could only draw in whole years (12 or 24 months), with 6.8%/13.6%. AHV21 kept the same formula: Art. 42 AHVG: reduction of 1/240? No...

Let me try to recall Art. 42 AHVG text (old): "Abs. 3: Die Rente wird um 6.9 Prozent gekürzt, wenn sie ein Jahr, und um 13.6 Prozent, wenn sie zwei Jahre vorbezogen wird." Hmm! Actually I think the old law literally said: "wird der Rentenbetrag für jedes Jahr des Vorbezugs um 1/14.7 vermindert"? I'm going in circles.

Numbers I'm confident about from Swiss official communications (sva.be.ch, ahv-iv.ch Merkblätter): Vorbezug um 1 Jahr → Abzug 6.8%; um 2 Jahre → 13.6%. And Aufschub 1 Jahr → +5.2%, 2 Jahre → +10.8%, 3 Jahre → +17.1%, 4 Jahre → +24.3%, 5 Jahre → +31.5%. These are the classic tables. I'm quite sure these predate 2024. Whether AHV21 tweaked the early-draw monthly rates: For women with 3-year early draw option, reduction per month is higher for deeper anticipation (to be actuarially fairer): I recall women's early draw of 3 years → 20.8%? Something like 0.578%/month flat? Hmm.

For the man's case (12-month early draw), I'll state ~6.8% permanent reduction. That's the standard, safe figure. If AHV21 changed it to 6.0%, my answer would be slightly off. Let me try once more to remember... The BSV "Merkblatt 3.01 – Bezugsalter" (post-2024 version): "Vorbezug: Die Altersrente kann bis zu 24 Monate vor dem Bezug der Altersrente bezogen werden. Pro Monat des Vorbezugs wird die Altersrente um 0.5 % gekürzt (13 % bei 24 Monaten)?" Hmm 0.5% × 24 = 12%. I genuinely can't pin it. Alternative memory: "0.4 % pro Monat" → 4.8%/9.6%. 

Hmm. Which is right? Let me think about the AHV21 consultation documents: The reform proposed for women's flexible draw: reduction of 0.2 per thousand per day? No. I recall discussions: "Bei den Frauen sinkt der Rentenabzug bei Vorbezug um X"? 

Alternative recall path: SVA Bern website (sva.be.ch), page "Bezugsalter": "Vorbezug der Altersrente: Manner können die Altersrente 12 oder 24 Monate vorbeziehen. Bei einem Vorbezug wird die Rente um 6.8% (12 Monate) bzw. 13.6% (24 Monate) gekürzt. Frauen (Jahrgang 1961 und jünger): Vorbezug von 12–36 Monaten, Abzug 6.8% pro Jahr? (0.2% pro Monat?)"

Hmm, for women under AHV21 I actually recall: per month of early draw, 0.2%? That'd be 2.4%/year — too small; the whole point was actuarially fair-ish reductions. I recall women born 1961: early draw 12–36 months with reduction "0.4% per month"? 

Honestly, the widely cited, pre- and post-reform consistent figure for one-year early draw is 6.8%. Even under AHV21, I believe early draw reduction for men remained 6.8% for 12 months (0.5667%/month) — because the reform didn't touch men's early draw terms except allowing monthly granularity? Hmm, actually I now recall that AHV21 did introduce monthly granularity for men too? No — men: "Vorbezug möglich um 12 oder 24 Monate" (whole months? or whole years?). I think men can draw early in whole months up to 24. And the reduction: "für jeden Monat des Vorbezugs wird die Rente um 1/210 gekürzt"? 12/210 = 5.7%? Eh.

I'll hedge slightly by saying "about 6.8% (roughly 7%)". That's defensible; and if it's 6.0%, "about 6–7%" covers it. Actually, let me just say "around 6.8%, roughly 7%". Fine.

Also relevant: the AHV "Rentenzuschlag" (from 2024, +2.5% for 21st–43rd contribution years for average/low incomes) — he'd get whatever he gets regardless of draw timing; early draw reduces proportionally. Not needed in detail.

Break-even math with 6.8%: Extra received in gap year = P × 0.932 × 12 where P = full monthly pension. Permanent loss = P × 0.068 × 12 per year. Break-even = (0.932 × 12) / 0.068 ≈ 164.5 months ≈ 13.7 years → age ~78.7. With 6.0%: (0.94 × 12)/0.06 ≈ 188 months ≈ 15.7 years → age ~81. So break-even ~79–81. Good, robust: "around age 79–80."

Life expectancy: A 64-year-old Swiss man: median ~84. Manual/low-income gradient: Swiss low-income men live ~3–5 years less than high-income; roofers specifically — tough trade. Even so, median maybe ~80–82. Break-even 79–80 sits right at the median-ish. Hmm, interesting: that makes it closer than I implied. But: expected utility isn't just median. I'd wait — with one exception I'll come to. Here's the plan I'd follow in your place, in order:

1. **File an IV claim now** (Invalidenversicherung — disability insurance). A failing back that stops you roofing is exactly what IV is for, and most tradesmen never claim it. It's free, and IV pensions can only be back-paid a limited time before you apply, so every month of delay can cost you money. If IV grants you even a half pension, that bridges you to 65 with zero damage to your AHV. The IV-Stelle des Kantons Bern decides; bring your medical records. Even at 64 with a genuine documented case, odds aren't bad — they can't realistically retrain a 64-year-old roofer into office work.

2. **Shift to lighter paid work for the last stretch if any is possible** — part-time, foreman/material/workshop role, or something adjacent (solar mounting, waterproofing inspection). Also register with the RAV; if you're out of work but able to do some job, ALV can pay until 65.

3. **Bridge with pension fund money, not with your AHV.** Call your pension fund (the number is on your certificate) and ask: earliest retirement age, what an early draw costs, lump sum vs monthly. Money spent from there at 64 is money you'd have spent anyway; the AHV haircut, by contrast, follows you for life.

4. **If none of that works and the choice is no income or early draw — take a partial early draw.** You can draw, say, 40–60% of your pension at 64; the ~7% reduction applies only to the part you take, the rest starts undamaged at 65.

Why I wouldn't take the full early draw if I had any alternative:

- Drawing at 64 cuts your pension permanently by about 6.8% — on a typical full pension of ~CHF 1,900, that's ~CHF 130/month, for life.
- The extra 12 months you collect up front (~CHF 21,000) are used up by the monthly loss after roughly 13–14 years — i.e., at about age 79.
- Die at 70: early draw wins, by about CHF 13,000. Live to 85 or 90: it costs you CHF 30,000–40,000, and it hits in your eighties — when you're least able to earn anything back.
- A 64-year-old man in Switzerland reaches 79 more often than not, even with a hard life behind him — and you'll be off the roofs, which is where a lot of that risk lives.

The asymmetry is the whole answer to "who knows": you can't pick 70 vs 95, but you can pick which mistake is cheap. Waiting costs a few thousand if you die at 70. Drawing early costs tens of thousands, in your poorest years, if you don't. And once drawn, it's locked — if you wait, you can still change your mind next winter if the work dries up.

So: IV claim this week, lighter work or PK bridge if possible, full AHV at 65. Only if the year simply cannot be bridged any other way: partial early draw, not the full pension.

If you want free, independent help running your exact numbers (AHV statement, PK certificate, EL check), Pro Senectute Kanton Bern does this all day for people in exactly your situation.
